record.paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: In causal supervised learning, invariant feature learning seeks features of data X that predict a label Y across environments, often interpreted as causal parents of Y rather than spurious style variables. How can the field build standardized, targeted benchmarks that deliberately vary spurious associations and environment shifts, so invariance-learning methods can be compared on a common test bed instead of only on method-specific toy experiments?

evidence.quote: Invariant feature learning (IFL) is the task of identifying features of our data X that are predictive of Y across a range of environments E.

Previous works in invariance learning often evaluate their suggested methods on novel toy experiments instead of a standardized test bed. As a result, practitioners cannot quickly determine the best approach for their problem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the setting of invariant feature learning in supervised classification. Let X be an input random variable taking values in a space X, let Y be a label random variable taking values in a space Y, and let E denote a finite or countable set of environments. For each e in E, assume there is a joint distribution P_e(X,Y) over X×Y. Invariant feature learning seeks a representation Φ: X → Z such that an optimal predictor f: Z → Y derived from Φ minimizes risk simultaneously across all environments, formally aiming to identify features capturing the causal parents of Y rather than spurious correlates whose relationship with Y varies with e.

Design a standardized, targeted benchmark suite for invariant feature learning that satisfies the following formal desiderata:

(1) The benchmark specifies a family F of data-generating processes {P_e}_{e ∈ E}, partitioned into training environments E_train and held-out test environments E_test, in which one can independently control:
   (a) the strength of spurious associations between non-causal features S(X) and Y (e.g., a tunable parameter ρ measuring Corr(S(X),Y | e)); and
   (b) the magnitude of distribution shift between training and test environments (e.g., a divergence d(P_e, P_{e'}) for e ∈ E_train, e' ∈ E_test).

(2) The benchmark defines a fixed evaluation protocol — a fixed set of train/test splits, model classes, and metrics — under which any candidate invariance-learning algorithm A produces a measurable score Score(A; F).

(3) The benchmark is sufficient, in the sense that for two algorithms A_1, A_2, the ordering of Score(A_1; F) and Score(A_2; F) reliably reflects their relative robustness to spurious correlations and environment shifts beyond F.

Construct such a benchmark family F and protocol, and prove (or empirically establish) that it yields comparisons among invariance-learning methods that are not achievable on isolated, method-specific toy experiments.
artifact.status_search_result: Benchmarks such as DomainBed, WILDS, and OoD-Bench have been proposed for distribution-shift and invariance evaluation, and partially address the demand for standardized targeted benchmarks. However, the broader problem of a benchmark suite that independently and systematically controls spurious-correlation strength and environment-shift magnitude for invariant feature learning remains active and is generally regarded as unresolved.

status_evidence.title: In Search of Lost Domain Generalization (DomainBed)
status_evidence.snippet: We present DomainBed, a testbed for domain generalization including seven multi-domain datasets, nine baseline algorithms, and three model selection criteria.
status_evidence.claim: Partial standardized benchmark for invariance/domain-generalization methods exists but does not fully meet the targeted-control desiderata.

status_evidence.title: WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts
status_evidence.snippet: WILDS is a curated benchmark of 10 datasets reflecting natural distribution shifts.
status_evidence.claim: Provides distribution-shift benchmarks but does not independently vary spurious-association strength.

status_evidence.title: OoD-Bench: Quantifying and Understanding Two Dimensions of Out-of-Distribution Generalization
status_evidence.snippet: We identify and measure two distinct kinds of distribution shift that are ubiquitous in OoD benchmarks: correlation shift and diversity shift.
status_evidence.claim: Recognizes the need to disentangle correlation and diversity shifts; problem of comprehensive targeted benchmarks remains open.
